title: Practice Passage 20: Hidden Cities Beneath the Forest

passage.title: Hidden Cities Beneath the Forest
passage.sub_title: How airborne laser scanning (LiDAR) is revealing massive, interconnected ancient urban centers beneath tropical rainforests.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] For many years, archaeologists believed that dense tropical forests prevented the development of large, organised cities. [A2] Thick vegetation made exploration extremely difficult, while heavy rainfall often damaged ancient structures. [A3] As a result, researchers assumed that only small communities had lived in many rainforest regions. [A4] Recent discoveries, however, have challenged this long-standing belief.

Paragraph B

[B1] One of the most significant advances has been the use of airborne laser scanning, often called LiDAR. [B2] Instead of relying only on photographs, this technology sends millions of laser pulses towards the ground from an aircraft. [B3] Some of these pulses pass through gaps in the tree canopy and reach the surface below. [B4] Computers then create detailed maps that reveal features hidden beneath the vegetation.

Paragraph C

[C1] Using this technology, researchers have identified roads, reservoirs, terraces, and building foundations that were previously invisible. [C2] Many of these structures appear to be connected through carefully planned networks. [C3] This suggests that ancient populations were larger and more organised than earlier generations of archaeologists had imagined. [C4] The discoveries have encouraged scholars to reconsider traditional theories about rainforest civilisations.

Paragraph D

[D1] Although LiDAR provides remarkable images, archaeologists emphasise that it cannot replace fieldwork. [D2] Maps produced by computers must still be checked on the ground. [D3] Excavations are necessary to determine the age, purpose, and history of each structure. [D4] Technology therefore assists archaeological research rather than replacing established scientific methods.

Paragraph E

[E1] The new discoveries have also highlighted the engineering abilities of ancient societies. [E2] Large water reservoirs indicate careful planning for dry seasons. [E3] Raised agricultural fields suggest that people modified difficult landscapes to improve food production. [E4] Such achievements demonstrate sophisticated environmental knowledge rather than simple survival techniques.

Paragraph F

[F1] Not everyone agrees about the interpretation of the new evidence. [F2] Some researchers believe certain structures were permanent settlements, while others argue that they were used only during particular seasons or ceremonies. [F3] Ongoing excavations continue to provide new information. [F4] Healthy scientific debate remains an essential part of archaeological research.

Paragraph G

[G1] Beyond archaeology, these discoveries influence how modern societies view tropical forests. [G2] They remind us that landscapes often considered untouched by humans may actually contain evidence of thousands of years of human activity. [G3] Understanding this relationship may help guide future conservation efforts. [G4] The hidden cities beneath today's forests continue to reshape our understanding of both history and the natural world.

C. creating underground tunnels.
